cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the part that was yours to do is done.
cells.act: tend it small and ask nothing of it
cells.ask: Give the coming week to what's actually still growing, and leave the finished thing where it lies. It won't need you.
cells.core:
You can finish a thing and actually open your hands. That's rarer than it sounds. Most people hold on past the end because letting go feels like losing, and you don't — when something you carried is done, you set it down and the next thing gets your attention. The room behind you clears and the room ahead fills.

There's one you'd hate to put down. You know which. Give the coming week to what's still alive instead, and leave the done thing where it lies. Some of what you've set down will look unfinished a while longer, and you'll be tempted to reach back for it because you can. Let it stay down. The open hand is what finds the next thing.
cells.sheetLine: You can finish something and open your hands.
cells.verb: setting down what has stopped being yours to carry
cells.place: at the moment the work is finished and the hands can open

cells.tense: You will have let go of this well before anyone could ask how it turned out.
cells.act: keep the steady light lit by attention, not flash
cells.ask: Stay with a piece of work you're halfway through for seven more days, through the days it feels pointless. No one to tell. Just keep returning to it.
cells.core:
You're letting go before things are finished, and calling it grace. Release comes early now — you step back from the half-made thing while it still needs hands on it, and the stepping back reads as modesty from where you stand. From outside, it looks like nothing ever gets the whole of you.

Here's the half you're skipping: something finished can be released clean, and something unfinished can't. Stay with a thing you're already in the middle of for a week without telling anyone it's hard. No plan, no announcement. If it holds, you'll find out what finishing feels like again. If it doesn't, that's information too — and you'll have learned it honestly instead of skipping ahead to goodbye.
cells.sheetLine: You let go early and call it grace.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door you already walked through, holding the handle.
cells.act: carry it without tightening around it
cells.ask: Whatever you're gripping right now, hold it this afternoon exactly as it is — no deciding, fixing, or sorting. If an answer comes, it comes.
cells.core:
Putting things down isn't available to you anymore. The grip has become the habit — you pick up what needs carrying and then don't stop, long past the point where anyone asked. The tiredness isn't from the weight. It's from the squeeze.

You don't have to release anything to get relief. You can carry it the same way without closing your fist. Take whatever you're gripping and hold it this afternoon exactly as it is — no sorting, no fixing, no verdict. If the answer arrives, it arrives. If it doesn't, the hour still counts. A body learns looser from looser, not from being told again to drop it. What you're gripping holds more than the thing — that's why the fist stays closed. The afternoon is what teaches the difference.
cells.sheetLine: The squeeze, not the weight, is what keeps you tired.
cells.verb: setting down what has stopped being yours to carry
cells.place: at the moment the work is finished and the hands can open

cells.tense: You are already past it and still describing the part where you were deciding.
cells.act: keep showing up to it without forcing a result
cells.ask: Show up to a question you think you're still deciding, without pushing it toward an answer, and notice what you already did.
cells.core:
You may have already let go of something and not noticed. Or you may be telling yourself you have while your hand is still closed — that part isn't clear even from inside you. Either way, the release or the grip is happening without your name on it, so it doesn't carry.

Slow it down. Take a question you believe you're still deciding, and spend a week simply showing up to it — no forcing it toward an answer, no verdict at the end. If you've already released it, the week shows you that, and you can stop dragging the story around. If you haven't, you'll find your hand still closed around it, which is worth knowing. Either way the aim becomes yours again. That's the part you can't get from guessing.
cells.sheetLine: You may already be past it, carrying the story anyway.
cells.verb: setting down what has stopped being yours to carry
cells.place: at the moment the work is finished and the hands can open

attempts.check: The record says the seat is Faith — purposeful release, letting go of what no longer serves — and I am claiming that release here is tied to finishing something, when the draw's own words are 'no longer serves' rather than 'complete.' A reader could reasonably say this is about grip and grasping, not about completion at all. The asks survive being wrong on that point: each one is a small act of tending or practice or holding that stands on its own. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line that makes release sound like a virtue to display rather than a thing a body does when it's done carrying something.
